query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) outside the well‐studied Nb–Ta matrices, the superconducting transition temperature is primarily governed by the average valence electron count (VEC), which tunes the density of states at the Fermi level and the electron–phonon coupling strength, rather than by the degree of chemical disorder.
generation.material_initial_state: A disordered solid-solution HEA containing at least five elements (each at ≥5 at.%) with a simple crystalline structure that exhibits conventional, phonon-mediated (isotropic s-wave) superconductivity.
generation.intervention: Systematically adjust the alloy composition by substituting one constituent with another to increase or decrease the average VEC while keeping the structural disorder similar.
generation.conditions: Low-temperature superconductivity measurements under ambient pressure with samples synthesized using controlled methods (e.g., melt processing or powder metallurgy) that yield comparable levels of compositional disorder.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniformly disordered crystalline lattice, where variations in VEC alter the electronic density-of-states at the Fermi level.
generation.mechanism: Altering the average VEC changes the electron density at the Fermi level, modulating the electron–phonon coupling strength according to BCS theory. An optimal VEC maximizes the density-of-states and electron–phonon interactions, thereby enhancing Tc. Deviations from this optimal electron count reduce the pairing interaction and lower Tc, independently of the high degree of chemical disorder inherent to HEAs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with compositions shifted toward an optimal VEC will display a higher superconducting transition temperature than the baseline alloy. In contrast, compositions with VEC values further from the optimum will have a reduced Tc, even though the overall structural disorder remains unchanged.
generation.baseline: The starting HEA with a measured Tc at a given non-optimal VEC, serving as the reference for assessing changes in electron count.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEAs that form a disordered solid solution and exhibit conventional, phonon-mediated (BCS) s-wave superconductivity. It may not apply in systems where magnetic pair-breaking or unconventional superconducting mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While analogous electron count dependencies have been suggested in related HEA systems, the precise quantitative relationship between VEC and Tc in these uncharacterized compositions remains uncertain. Additionally, subtle local ordering effects or variations in electron scattering rates might also influence superconductivity.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of HEA samples with identical processing conditions and comparable disorder but with systematically varied average valence electron counts (via controlled elemental substitutions).
measurements: Determine Tc using resistivity and magnetic susceptibility measurements.
Characterize the electronic density-of-states near the Fermi level, for example via photoemission or tunneling spectroscopy.
Confirm the structural phase and degree of disorder using X-ray diffraction or electron microscopy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if no systematic correlation between the average VEC and Tc is observed, or if modifications in VEC do not correspond to the predicted changes in the density-of-states and electron–phonon coupling strength despite comparable structural disorder.

Superconductivity in a uranium containing high entropy alloy

Abstract: High entropy alloys (HEA) are an unusual class of materials where mixtures of elements are stochastically arrayed on a simple crystalline lattice. These systems exhibit remarkable functionality, often along several distinct axes: e.g., the examples [TaNb]1-x(TiZrHf)x are high strength and damage resistant refractory metals that also exhibit superconductivity with large upper critical fields. Here we report the discovery of an f-electron containing HEA, [TaNb]0.31(TiUHf)0.69, which is the first to include an actinide ion. Similar to the Zr-analogue, this material crystallizes in a body-centered cubic lattice with the lattice constant a = 3.41(1) Å and exhibits phonon mediated superconductivity with a transition temperatures Tc ≈ 3.2 K and upper critical fields Hc2 ≈ 6.4 T. These results expand this class of materials to include actinide elements, shows that superconductivity is robust in this sub-group, and opens the path towards leveraging HEAs as functional waste forms for a variety of radioisotopes.

Evidence for isotropic s-wave superconductivity in high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEA) form through the random arrangement of five or more chemical elements on a crystalline lattice. Despite the significant amount of resulting compositional disorder, a subset of HEAs enters a superconducting state below critical temperatures, Tc<10 K. The superconducting properties of the known HEAs seem to suffice a Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) description, but little is known about their superconducting order parameter and the microscopic role of disorder. We report on magnetic susceptibility measurements on films of the superconducting HEA (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x for characterizing the lower and upper critical fields Hc,1(T) and Hc,2(T), respectively as a function of temperature T. Our resulting analysis of the Ginzburg–Landau coherence length and penetration depth demonstrates that HEAs of this type are single-band isotropic s-wave superconductors in the dirty limit.
